name: Tonsillitis
definition: An infection of the tonsils, most often caused by a virus and sometimes by bacteria, that brings a sore throat, painful swallowing and fever.
overview: The tonsils are two small lumps of tissue at the back of the throat. Tonsillitis is usually caused by a virus, such as the kind behind a cold, though bacteria such as group A streptococcus (strep throat) can also be responsible. It is common in children, teenagers and young adults. Symptoms usually ease within three to four days, though they can last longer, and most people are better within about a week. Viral cases usually clear up on their own, and antibiotics are considered only for bacterial cases.
causes: A viral infection, such as a cold or flu virus, is the usual cause
A bacterial infection, most often a strain called group A streptococcus (strep throat)
Most of the infections that lead to tonsillitis, such as colds and flu, are contagious and spread between people
riskFactors: Age: it is most common in children, teenagers and young adults
Close contact with people who have infections
signs: White spots of pus on the tonsils in some people
Swollen, tender glands in the neck
complications: Quinsy, a pocket of pus between a tonsil and the throat wall, which is rare but potentially serious
Rheumatic fever following group A streptococcal infection, which is rare in developed countries
Infection that does not respond to antibiotics by mouth and worsens, which may need hospital treatment with antibiotics given into a vein
Complications are rare overall and usually occur only when the cause is bacterial
diagnosis: A doctor can usually tell that a person has tonsillitis by asking about the symptoms and looking in the throat. A swab test may be used to see whether bacteria are causing the infection. A blood test for glandular fever may be done if symptoms are severe or do not go away. For sore throats in general, NICE guidance describes two scoring tools, FeverPAIN and Centor, that help clinicians identify people more likely to benefit from antibiotics.
treatment: Tonsillitis caused by a virus usually clears up on its own, so treatment is mostly about easing symptoms. Self-care described by the NHS includes paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, plenty of rest and fluids, and gargling with warm salty water. A pharmacist can advise on which treatments suit a person or child, and the NHS advises that aspirin is not given to children under 16. If a bacterial cause is found, a GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics taken by mouth. NICE says antibiotics give only a small benefit for sore throat, and that a delayed prescription is generally recommended unless symptoms are very severe or the person is vulnerable to complications. Removal of the tonsils (tonsillectomy) is described by the NHS as usually reserved for severe tonsillitis that keeps coming back.
prevention: NHS guidance on limiting the spread of infection suggests washing hands often, especially after touching the nose or mouth and before handling food, coughing and sneezing into tissues and throwing them away promptly, avoiding close contact with people who have infections, and not sharing glasses or utensils with someone who is ill.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for signs of quinsy: a severe sore throat that gets worse quickly, swelling in the mouth or throat, difficulty speaking, being unable to swallow or breathing difficulties, and the NHS advises not to drive there. A GP appointment is advised when tonsillitis symptoms have not gone away within about a week or when throat infections keep coming back. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not start to improve after a week, or the person becomes very unwell, and NHS 111 can advise when the surgery is closed.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of tonsillitis?
sections.body:
The usual symptoms of tonsillitis are a sore throat, pain when swallowing, earache and fever. The tonsils may look swollen and red, and some people have white spots of pus on them. The glands in the neck can become swollen and tender.

Symptoms typically get worse over two to three days and then gradually settle. The NHS says they usually ease within three to four days, although they can last longer. NHS inform describes tonsillitis as an illness that usually gets better on its own within a week.

A sore throat is a very common problem, and tonsillitis is one cause of it. NICE uses the term acute sore throat to cover tonsillitis and pharyngitis together, and describes it as an illness that tends to clear up by itself and is often set off by a viral infection of the upper airways.

sections.heading: What causes tonsillitis?
sections.body:
Most cases of tonsillitis are caused by a virus, such as the viruses behind colds and flu. Bacteria can also be responsible, and the usual bacterial cause is a strain called group A streptococcus, which is also behind strep throat.

The NHS says tonsillitis itself is not contagious, but most of the infections that lead to it, for example colds and flu, are. This is why close contact with people who are unwell is linked to catching the infections that can cause it. Tonsillitis is most common in children, teenagers and young adults.

Telling a viral from a bacterial cause matters because treatment differs. Viral cases usually clear up on their own, while a GP may prescribe antibiotics when bacteria are the cause. NICE notes that people with a streptococcal infection are more likely to benefit from antibiotics than others with a sore throat.

sections.heading: How is tonsillitis diagnosed?
sections.body:
A doctor can usually tell that a person has tonsillitis by asking about the symptoms and looking in the throat. A swab test may be used to see whether bacteria are causing the infection. A blood test for glandular fever may be done if symptoms are severe or do not go away.

For sore throats in general, NICE recommends that clinicians use one of two scoring tools, FeverPAIN or Centor, to pick out the people who may be more likely to benefit from antibiotics. Low scores point towards offering no antibiotic, while higher scores lead the clinician to consider an immediate or a back-up prescription.

Medical help is advised if symptoms last longer than the usual few days without improving, or if they are severe, for example when a person cannot eat or drink. Difficulty breathing is an emergency, and the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

sections.heading: How is tonsillitis treated?
sections.body:
Because viral tonsillitis usually clears up on its own, treatment is mostly about easing symptoms. The NHS suggests paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, plenty of rest and fluids, and gargling with warm salty water. NICE also lists paracetamol and ibuprofen as options for pain or fever. A pharmacist can advise which treatments suit a person or child, and the NHS advises that aspirin is not given to children under 16.

Antibiotics are not routine. A GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics by mouth when a bacterial cause is found. NICE guidance aims to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use and the spread of antibiotic resistance. It says antibiotics bring only a small benefit for sore throat and that withholding them rarely leads to complications. A delayed prescription is generally recommended unless symptoms are very severe or the person is vulnerable to complications, and people at high risk of serious illness should be offered antibiotics straight away. If treatment by mouth fails and symptoms worsen, a GP may refer a person to hospital for antibiotics given into a vein.

sections.heading: What are the complications of tonsillitis?
sections.body:
Complications are rare and usually happen only when the infection is bacterial. The best known is quinsy, also called a peritonsillar abscess, in which a pocket of pus builds up between a tonsil and the wall of the throat, usually after a bacterial infection spreads from the tonsil. It is a rare but potentially serious complication.

Signs of quinsy include a severe sore throat that gets worse quickly, swelling in the mouth or throat, difficulty speaking, being unable to swallow, and breathing difficulties. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for these signs, and not driving to hospital. NHS inform adds that quinsy needs prompt review by a GP, and that a sore throat that worsens very quickly may point to it.

Rheumatic fever, which follows infection with group A streptococcus, is another complication, but it is rare in developed countries. Using antibiotics for viral tonsillitis does not significantly reduce the risk of quinsy and is not routinely recommended.

sections.heading: When is tonsil removal considered?
sections.body:
Removal of the tonsils is called a tonsillectomy. The NHS says it is usually done only if a person has severe tonsillitis that keeps coming back. NHS inform describes it as an option for long-running or recurring cases, usually considered after several severe episodes over a long period or when repeated bouts disrupt normal activities.

Leaflets from NHS hospital trusts describe the operation as done under general anaesthetic, with the tonsils taken out through the mouth, so there is no cut on the outside of the neck. They describe a sore throat that can last for up to about two weeks afterwards, and they treat fresh bleeding after the operation as a reason to go to A&E. Criteria for surgery vary between areas, and the usual next step for someone who keeps getting tonsillitis is a GP review of the episodes against local criteria.

faqs.a: The NHS says tonsillitis itself is not contagious, but most of the infections that cause it, such as colds and flu, are contagious. NHS guidance on limiting spread includes washing hands often, coughing and sneezing into tissues, and not sharing glasses or utensils with someone who is ill.

Symptoms typically get worse over two to three days and then settle. The NHS says they usually ease within three to four days but can last longer. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms do not start to improve after a week, worsen rapidly or significantly, or the person becomes very unwell, and a GP appointment is the usual route.

Viral tonsillitis usually clears up on its own. A GP may prescribe antibiotics when bacteria are the cause. NICE says antibiotics give only a small benefit for sore throat, and that scoring tools help decide between no antibiotic, a back-up prescription or an immediate prescription.

faqs.q: When does tonsillitis need urgent help?
faqs.a: Signs of quinsy include a severe sore throat that gets worse quickly, swelling in the mouth or throat, difficulty speaking, being unable to swallow or breathing difficulties. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for these signs, and not driving there. A GP appointment is advised for symptoms that have not gone away within about a week or throat infections that keep coming back.

faqs.q: Is tonsil removal the usual treatment?
faqs.a: No, the NHS says tonsil removal is usually done only if severe tonsillitis keeps coming back. NHS inform describes it as considered after several severe episodes over a long period or when repeated episodes disrupt normal activities. A GP can review the episodes against local criteria, which vary between areas.
